prompt: Checkout requires successful responses from Payments, Inventory and Fraud. Each service can fail independently. A colleague says adding Fraud cannot reduce availability because Payments was already the least available dependency. Which explanation is right?

options.text: Correct: only the least available dependency affects checkout
options.explanation: Wrong. A failure of any required service can fail checkout, including a failure while every other service is healthy.
Wrong. Redundancy needs alternatives that can serve the same purpose. Fraud is another required result.

options.text: Fraud adds another way for checkout to fail
options.explanation: Correct. Checkout needs every dependency to succeed. An independent Fraud outage can fail requests that would otherwise have succeeded.

options.text: The answer is always found by adding outage percentages
options.explanation: Wrong. Overlapping outages must not be counted twice. Independence permits a product model; shared causes require a different analysis.

workedExample:
1. Identify the success condition: all three required responses must succeed.
2. Consider a Fraud outage while Payments and Inventory are healthy. Checkout now fails, so Fraud adds exposure.
3. The exact combined availability depends on each service and how failures overlap. Independence gives a useful model, but shared networks or databases can correlate failures.
4. Move work off the response path only when the product does not need its result before responding.

prompt: A product page calls 10 backend services **in parallel** and waits for all of them before rendering. Each service answers in about 50 ms 99% of the time, but 1% of its calls take about 1 second, independently of the others. Users report that roughly 1 page load in 10 takes about a second. Every service dashboard shows only 1% slow calls. What explains the gap?

options.text: Measurement noise: if each service is slow 1% of the time, pages must be slow about 1% of the time
options.explanation: Wrong. That would hold if the page waited for one particular service. It waits for all ten, so it is slow whenever **any** one of them is slow, which is far more likely than one specific call being slow.

options.text: The services must be slow together, because a page is only slow when all 10 calls are slow
options.explanation: Wrong. All ten being slow at once would be vanishingly rare (0.01 multiplied by itself ten times). The page needs only one slow call to be slow, because it waits for every result.

options.text: The page waits for the slowest of 10 calls, so it is slow if any one is slow: about 1 load in 10
options.explanation: Correct. All ten calls are fast only about 90% of the time (0.99 multiplied by itself ten times is about 0.904), so roughly 9.6% of page loads include at least one 1-second call. This is tail amplification: per-service tails become common at the page level.

options.text: Parallel calls add their latencies, so ten 50 ms calls take 500 ms and push the page towards a second
options.explanation: Wrong. Parallel calls overlap; the page waits for the slowest one, not the sum. Adding durations applies to sequential, dependent calls.

workedExample:
1. The page waits for all ten results in parallel, so one slow required result delays the page.
2. Each dashboard measures one service. The page is exposed to the slow-call risk of every required service, so its slow requests can be much more common.
3. Parallel durations overlap; sequential dependent durations add. These are different critical paths.
4. Consider omitting optional results after a timeout or moving unnecessary response-path work to a queue. Hedged requests can reduce some tail delays but add load and require safe duplicate handling; they need workload-specific controls.
